blocks.text: **And when we say you should daven to G-d and not to His middos**, the text speaks of **even His middos ha'atzmiyim** (His essential attributes). So we should not think that G-d is essentially a nice guy, and that you should just give a sob story and He will give you what you want.

blocks.title: The sob story
blocks.text: Go to a person with a sob story, and he knows what you are trying to do: you just think he is a nice guy and he will feel bad for you. "That's called being manipulative, and he's gonna slap you." Instead of getting *chesed*, he will *davka* do the opposite, because you are not recognizing him. If you try to play off somebody's nature, say he is nice, with reverse psychology or a sob story or some trick like that, you are really trying to manipulate him. It is the same as taking the guy's hand, reaching it into his pocket and making it take out the wallet and give you the money. You are not recognizing that he is there and choosing to do it; you are treating him like a thing, "this piece of meat", and it is a very big insult, and "you deserve to get punched in the face."

That is what happens when a person does not recognize G-d. It says that they *daven* asking for a *chesed chinam* (an unearned kindness): they realize that G-d does not have to do it. You are asking Him: To You, I know, I realize You do not have to do it, nothing I can do can make You do it, and I am just asking You sincerely, would You please do me a favor. That brings out the *ratzon*, but you have to recognize the *etzem*.

**Because really the Atzmus Ein Sof is not affected in any of these middos really. It's really higher than that.** **This is what we say that You connect them all, You unite all the sefiros**, *Ant* *davka*: **davka G-d Himself, His etzem**. **This is like we say that You are one, but not the cheshbon of the ten sefiros**: G-d is higher than all the ten *sefiros*. And *davka* because He is higher than all of them and not stuck, He can unite them all, because to Him the limitations do not exist; they are not really different things, it is really just His *etzem*.

Then He was *metzamtzem* His *etzem* to reveal it in different ways, "like masks and tools and stuff." But not only that: it is true that they all come from His *etzem*, and they are really one thing. He is the kind guy, and He is the mean guy. *Ant hu*: it is really Him. So the kindness and the meanness are really the same thing; it looks different only to you.

That is the whole thing talked about in section 11. If you say the *chesed* goes all the way up to the *etzem*, and the *gevura* goes all the way up to the *etzem*, you must say that they are really one *etzem*, not two separate things. Being mean and being nice? Yes, it is really Him doing whatever He wants. There is no real thing of being kind: what does it mean, you are being kind? That does not mean anything. You create some form or pattern that defines being kind, but really you are doing what you think is the best thing to do. There is no real difference between the two; like addition and subtraction, they look like opposites, but they are not.

blocks.title: Head souls and foot souls
blocks.text: It is like all the Jews: in the *pnimiyus* they are really all the same thing. Later they have different souls, head souls, hand souls, heart souls and feet souls, with different jobs, serving G-d in different ways, and at first glance they look different, and they can hate each other. A head guy says the main thing is to do *hisbonenus* to understand *Chassidus*. A foot guy says the main thing is to go do *mivtzoim* (outreach campaigns). The head guy hates going on *mivtzoim* and likes learning *Chassidus*; the foot guy likes going on *mivtzoim* and hates learning *Chassidus*. They hate each other because each thinks the other is contradicting him. And really what they are doing is each using his *koach* to serve G-d as best he can.

sections.title: Two equal, infinite lines: the Kav as a measuring stick for the Essence's will
sections.summary: In the *Atzmus*, the power to hide and limit and the power to spread and unite are two lines, equal and both infinite, and so they stay equal when they come down in the *Kav*: every change, from weekday to *Shabbos*, is one power showing as *chesed* and *gevura*. The *Kav* is a *hiyuli* like a measuring stick, and any exception shows that the system is only His choice.

blocks.text: **So too, from etzem Ein Sof comes the koach hagvul v'hamida** (the power of limit and measure), in the *reshimu* in the *Kav*, **and because of this reshimu it's called kav hamida**: G-d chose that it should be a certain way, because, just as G-d can do whatever He wants... **And they're interdependent**: G-d can do what He wants, so He can make a system and He can break a system.

**Like explains elsewhere about the inyan of chesed and gevura in the Atzmus of the Ein Sof**: first there is **the koach hagvul, the gevura, which is that He's able to limit and hide within Himself higher and higher to no end, His etzem or**, and make it look like a *reshimu*, a totally separate, limited thing, totally outside of His power, so that you see no connection between things and it all just seems totally set.

blocks.title: Shake the lulav; the wall says no
blocks.text: In the light you see that there is an inner *nekuda* uniting it, a *kavana* (intention). But once it comes to the *reshimu*, no: there are no deeper meanings, no inner intentions. "All I want is take a *lulav* and shake it. That's it." With the *hadassim* and the *aravos* and the *esrog*, and shake it. You say, but what does He really mean, what does He want? No, that is it, there is nothing else, that is what He wants, and everything else is hidden. Or you go to a wall and try to walk through it, and the wall says no. That's it, you cannot walk through. Why? "No whys, no buts, that's just the way it is." That is the *teva*, "the magical word *teva*", of the wall. But really that is coming from the *Atzmus*; it is *mamash* like the *Atzmus*: a *metzius* on its own, with no reason before it or after it. That is the *yesh gamur* that comes from the *yesh amiti*.

**That's the Ein Sof that goes up to no end**, **and there's also hispashtus ha'or down to no end**: **that through the Kav it comes down through the reshimu and G-d reveals Himself in the world more and more**.

blocks.title: The Rebbe's sichos
blocks.text: Now which side is *chesed* and which is *gevura*? It does not really matter, because *chesed* and *gevura* are interchangeable: when you face somebody, your right side is facing his left side. It is a totally relative term. Say the Rebbe comes out and says lots of *sichos* (talks). In a way you say that is a *chesed*, because he is teaching us a lot. But on the other hand that is really a *gevura*, because he has to limit his *sechel*: instead of learning and doing things on his level, "he has to come down to this really stupid level, and talk really slow, and really stupidly," and sit there for hours to explain things to us, and then they do not get it, so he has to do it again. So it is a really big *gevura*, especially for him.

sensitivity.publishable: Now which side is *chesed* and which is *gevura*? It does not really matter, because *chesed* and *gevura* are interchangeable: when you face somebody, your right side is facing his left side. It is a totally relative term. Say the Rebbe comes out and says lots of *sichos* (talks). In a way you say that is a *chesed*, because he is teaching us a lot. But on the other hand that is really a *gevura*, because he has to limit his *sechel*: instead of learning and doing things on his level, he has to come down to our level, speak slowly and simply, and sit there for hours to explain things to us, and then they do not get it, so he has to do it again. So it is a really big *gevura*, especially for him.

blocks.title: The Rebbe's locked room
blocks.text: On the other hand, when the Rebbe locks up his room, or does not come out for a long time, busy learning or doing whatever he is doing, in a way that is a big *chesed*, a vacation: he can do things on his level, a much higher level, where everything is much more *b'gilui* to him. But to us it is a big *gevura*, because we do not appreciate it. So Rabbi Walters thinks that is why the Mitteler Rebbe does not say here which one is *chesed* and which is *gevura*: sometimes it is explained one way, sometimes the other.

That is what is explained here: the names are superimposed, the system is superimposed, and in a way that makes it easier to understand. You can start learning *Chassidus* because they draw you a map: there is *Atzilus*, *Beriya*, *Yetzira* and *Asiya*, and there are the ten *sefiros*, put in three lines for you. It becomes very tangible, not so abstract; you can memorize it and feel, "I'm understanding something." But on the other hand it totally *maalim* (conceals): it is like a *masach* that is *mavdil* (a screen that separates), and it totally covers over the *etzem*. It makes you think these crazy stupid things, that it is like this machine, all these weird ideas people have, and it totally covers over the *etzem* of it.

When you just explain the thing and people really understand what it is talking about, it is much easier. That is why people have all these questions all the time, that here it says one thing and here something else, as if it contradicts: they do not get that it is not like this system. Even all the terms, *chesed* and *gevura*, are relative and really interchangeable: *chesed* is really *gevura* and *gevura* is really *chesed*, a superimposed thing; all these distinctions are really not true. But there is a truth to them. It is not totally bogus, and not totally true either; it is not set in stone. It is like a person deciding to come down and do things in a system: the system itself is a choice, so it is really not a system. It is really both at the same time.

blocks.text: **These two lines, these two abilities are exactly equal**, *shekulin*: **they're both completely infinite, equally infinite**. G-d can make Himself transcend everything infinitely and be above all definitions and all levels, all the way above even the ten *sefiros* of *Yachid*, above *Atzmus*, above anything. "Don't tell Him what to do." If you can name it, He can go above it; even if you cannot name it, He can go above it. And it is also infinite going down. So the two lines are equal, and both are infinite.

Therefore, since in the *Atzmus* these two are equal, G-d is *kol yachol* both ways equally: He can transcend everything, and He can limit Himself down to the smallest thing and put His whole *etzem* there, and to Him it is all the same. So even when He does things in a small way, as in the *Kav*, and these two *middos* now come out in a limited way instead of an infinite way, they are still both equal. The *Kav* can measure things as big as G-d wants or as small as G-d wants. Though it all happens now on a smaller scale, according to the *mekablim* and not according to His essential ability, He can still do it as much as He wants either way; they are both equal: **to either limit and divide and separate, or to connect and unite**.

**And so too all the changes in the light and the hamshacha**, **whether it's coming more or less**, **like changes from time to time**, **like change from the week to Shabbos and Yom Tov**, when there are different *yichudim* (unions) going on, and from the time of the *Beis HaMikdash* to the time of *galus*: **it's all really one power, which is equal**, **which is revealed in two opposite ways**. It is really one *etzem* thing revealed as two opposites, *chesed* and *gevura*: G-d can do whatever He wants, and that is revealed as being able to make the rules and to break the rules.

So what is the difference between the week and *Shabbos*? In the week G-d makes it that there is a system, and you have to follow the system and be *mevarer* (refine) things. On *Shabbos* He reveals that we are really above the system. And really the *etzem* is above either, so He can choose to do it this way or that way; it is the *gilui* of the same thing. That is the whole point: G-d can do whatever He wants, and the way the *etzem* is revealed is that it transcends everything and that it goes into everything, two ways of revealing the same *etzem*. *Shabbos* within the rest of the week, and what there is in *Shabbos* that comes from the week, shows you the *yichud* of the two there.

**They both come from the koach and the first or of the Atzmus Ein Sof**, **as it is essentially to itself**. Since essentially it is, *kaviyachol* (as it were), both ways, in the *Kav* it is revealed that it has both things.

blocks.title: The measuring stick does not limit the house
blocks.text: **This is like we explained before**, in section 14: **the Kav is a hiyuli compared to the rest of the hishtalshelus, which is like the shetach** (the area), **according to the etzem hamashpia that he can bring out the shetach however he wants**. When you have a measuring stick, it does not limit the house: you can keep measuring and make the house as big as you want, or as small as you want.

blocks.title: The teacher's compromise
blocks.text: **Just that in your etzem it's in a much bigger way, the ability that you have.** **But when it comes on the Kav**, **now the same thing is coming out in a limited way**. Like the teacher: he understands the idea in an infinite way, both ways. He sees the *nekuda*, how it transcends all the explanations, and he can also put it into infinite explanations. Either way he can go infinite: he can make it one *nekuda* that includes every possible *inyan*, or bring it into infinite explanations, totally separate, each a different thing, more explanations and more *meshalim*, each with its own *inyan*, different from every other, and he could do that infinitely. But when he *b'poel mamash* (actually) explains it to a student, he makes some sort of compromise that is not infinite either way. Yet it is really coming from that same thing; only now it comes according to the *mekabel*.

**Therefore both the tzimtzum and hispashtus, the Kav is really coming from there.** That is why, if he wants, he can be *maarich* (extend) the *inyan* back to the *etzem*, if he talks to somebody on his level, or bring it all the way down to a little kid, and it is all the same thing. That is the point: G-d can do whatever He wants, and it is revealed through these two things. Though G-d reveals *tzimtzum* and *hispashtus*, *chesed* and *gevura*, within the *hishtalshelus* only in a limited way, it is really coming from the *etzem*, that He can do whatever He wants.

Within the ten *sefiros* we usually see G-d doing whatever He wants only a little: a little more, a little less. But the fact that He can make any change shows that He is already above the whole system, even if you say it is just a little change. You say, "Oh, I'm really keeping the laws and the system, I'm just making a little exception." No: "once you make a little exception, that's really revealing that the whole thing is bogus," that there is really no system and there are no rules, that you are doing whatever you want and there are really no limits, or else you would not be able to make these decisions.

Really, when you go to a store and the person says, "Well, I don't have the jurisdiction, you have to go to my manager," it is not really true, because he is a person and has a certain power, and he could just make an exception. Maybe he does not want to, because he is afraid he would get in trouble, but he could do it. "When you go to a cashier at, you know, Walmart or something like that, they could really do whatever they want." They do not have to follow the rules if they do not want to. Maybe they will get in trouble, but they are human. "They forget that they are sometimes, but they can do whatever they want."

blocks.text: And why is a manager any better? The manager is not really any better; they just set up a system in which the manager is allowed and this person is not. Really, what is the difference? It is just making a judgment call, and I can make the same judgment call. There is no inherent reason that this person should be the manager and I should not; maybe I am more qualified and smarter and can make better decisions. But part of what you decide is that he is going to be in charge and I am not, and that is it, you have to listen to the orders. So the system is that you decided to make a system. It is really not a system: the system is only that you decided to make a system. *V'dai l'mevin*.

reviewQuestions.question: If the *reshimu* holds G-d's whole *etzem*, why does a rock, a tree or ink on paper show nothing of Him by itself, and where is He seen instead?
How can G-d "decide to be a squirrel" without being trapped in it, and why does that make bowing to a thing *avoda zara*?
What two opposite things are found in the *Kav*, and why is "if you make the rules, you can break the rules" the answer?
Why, in the *mashal* of the newlyweds' house, does every request end with the husband, and what does that teach about change in the *hishtalshelus*?
Why should one *daven* to G-d and not to His *middos*, and what is wrong with a sob story?
In what sense are the two lines of limiting and spreading "equal", and how does the difference between the week and *Shabbos* show it?
